---
title: C# Types
topic: [Programming]
subtopic: [NET]
summary: "How C# types define shape, behavior, and value versus reference assignment semantics."
tags: [FolderNote]
publish: true
status: Creation
priority: Medium
level: ["4"]
qard-deck: "Programming"
qard-topic: "NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Types"
flashcard_uid: "a5c39ae2"
created: "2026-02-10T16:03:55.000Z"
modified: "2026-10-28T12:33:42.000Z"
---

A C# type defines what values exist, which operations are valid, and what assignment copies. Value types copy their contained value. Reference types copy a reference to one object. That distinction controls aliasing and equality long before stack-versus-heap details matter.

The folder separates the main forms. Classes and record classes are reference types. Structs and record structs are value types. Strings, delegates, and events add specialized behavior on top of the same type system.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Copy and Storage Boundaries

- **Assignment:** a value-type assignment copies every field. Reference fields inside that value still point to the same objects. A reference-type assignment copies the object reference, so both variables can observe mutations to one instance.
- **Arguments:** parameters are passed by value unless marked `ref`, `out`, or `in`. Passing a reference type by value copies the reference, not the object.
- **Storage:** value types may live inline inside heap objects and arrays. References may be local variables. Declaration kind does not dictate one physical location.
- **Boxing:** conversion from a value type to `object` or an interface value copies it into a box. Constrained generic calls can often avoid that allocation. Nullable value types box differently: a populated `Nullable<T>` boxes its underlying `T` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating a box.

# Pitfalls

- **Hidden aliases.** Several references can point at one mutable object. Ownership must be clear. Shared models are easier to reason about when immutable.
- **Mutable value copies.** A property, indexer, or `foreach` variable usually exposes a struct copy. Mutation may be rejected by the compiler or affect only the copy. Readonly structs and whole-value replacement keep that boundary visible.
- **Equality chosen by accident.** Classes use reference equality unless they define another contract. Record classes and record structs synthesize value equality, while ordinary structs inherit field-based default equality. Domain identity should decide, not syntax convenience.

# Tradeoffs

- **Class or struct:** a class makes shared identity and inheritance available. A struct gives value-copy semantics and can avoid a separate allocation, but large copies and boxing may cost more.
- **Record class or conventional class:** records fit data whose contents define equality. Identity-rich entities usually need conventional class semantics.
- **Interface or constrained generic:** an interface value gives runtime polymorphism but boxes a struct. A constrained generic can preserve static typing and avoid the box.

# Examples

```csharp
var h = new Holder { Counter = new Counter { Value = 0 } };

// Property access returns a copy of the struct value.
h.Counter.Inc();
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 0

// Fix: replace the whole value after mutation.
var c = h.Counter;
c.Inc();
h.Counter = c;
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 1

public struct Counter
{
    public int Value;
    public void Inc() => Value++;
}

public sealed class Holder
{
    public Counter Counter { get; set; }
}
```

The direct `h.Counter.Inc()` call compiles, but it mutates the temporary value returned by the property and then discards that copy. A direct field assignment such as `h.Counter.Value = 1` is rejected with CS1612. Reading the value into `c`, mutating it, and assigning it back persists the change.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: d8eb59cf-ad2d-43be-954f-44db23f34d38 -->
> [!qard]- Why might changing a struct inside `foreach` not update the collection, and how can it be fixed?
> In an ordinary (non-`ref`) `foreach`, each struct element reaches the loop body as a copy held in a read-only iteration variable. Changes to the copy's own fields never reach the stored element.
>
> - Assigning the iteration variable, or one of its fields, is rejected by the compiler.
> - Calling a mutating method on it compiles, but the method changes the copy's fields rather than the stored element's, so the update is silently lost.
>
> The copy is shallow. When a field of the struct refers to an object, such as a `List<T>`, the copy and the stored element refer to the same object. A change made to that object through the copy, such as adding an item, therefore remains visible through the collection. Only changes to the struct's own field values are lost.
>
> The stored elements can be updated in two ways:
>
> - **Indexed write-back:** a loop by index reads `items[i]` into a local, changes the local and assigns it back to `items[i]`, replacing the whole element value.
> - **`ref` iteration:** when the collection exposes its elements by reference, as `Span<T>` does, `foreach (ref var item in span)` makes `item` an alias for the stored element, so changes apply in place.
>
> Mutable structs make this mistake easy. Immutable structs, updated by creating a new value and assigning it back, keep the copy boundary visible.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

<!-- qard-id: b89f32ef-f23d-488d-a26a-78ebe0051826 -->
> [!qard]- Where does boxing commonly happen, and how can it be reduced?
> Boxing happens wherever a value type is converted to `object` or to an interface it implements. The runtime allocates an object on the managed heap and copies the value into it. A nullable value type is boxed according to its contents: a populated `int?` boxes its underlying `int` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating.
>
> Common places:
>
> - **`object`-typed variables, collections and parameters:** `object o = 42;`, adding an `int` to a `List<object>` or an `ArrayList`, or passing a struct to a parameter of type `object`.
> - **Interface-typed variables and parameters:** assigning a struct to an `IComparable` variable, or passing it where an interface type is declared.
>
> Each box is a separate heap allocation that the garbage collector must later reclaim. The box also holds a copy, so later changes to the original value do not affect it.
>
> Ways to reduce boxing:
>
> - **Generic collections and APIs:** a generic collection such as `List<int>` is specialized for `int`, so adding an element stores the value without converting it to `object`.
> - **Constrained generics instead of interface-typed parameters:** a method such as `Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>` can call `CompareTo` on a struct argument without converting it to the interface type, provided the struct itself implements that member.
>
> These changes matter mainly in frequently executed code. They justify extra API complexity where profiling shows boxing allocations are significant.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

<!-- qard-id: d5bda60c-1799-4e4a-ab36-7624ae085e3a -->
> [!qard]- When should a type be a `struct`, `class`, or `record class`?
> The choice follows the semantics the type needs. A `struct` fits a small value that is copied field by field, a `class` fits an object with its own identity, and a `record class` fits a reference type whose contents define its equality. Copying, mutation and measured allocation costs then confirm or adjust that semantic choice.
>
> | Aspect | `struct` | `class` | `record class` |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Assignment and passing | Copies every field, so each variable holds its own field values. The copy is shallow: a reference-type field copies only the reference, so both copies can still point to one object. | Copies a reference, so several variables can share and observe one object. | Copies a reference, as a class does. |
> | Default equality | `Equals` is true when both have the same type and the same stored values. | Equality holds only when both references point to the same object, even if every field matches. | Compiler-generated `Equals` and `==` compare the type and member values. The generated `GetHashCode` compares nothing; it returns hash codes compatible with that equality, so equal records hash equally. |
> | Mutation | A change to a copy's own fields affects only that copy, so such changes are easy to lose. A change to an object reached through a reference field is visible through every copy that shares it. | A change is visible through every reference to the object. | Positional properties are init-only by default, and a `with` expression creates a modified shallow copy whose reference-type members still point to the same objects. |
> | Allocation and cost | Stored inline in the variable, field or array element that holds it, with no allocation of its own. Large values make every copy expensive, and boxing allocates. | One heap allocation per instance. | One heap allocation per instance, as with a class. |
> | Inheritance | Cannot derive from another struct or class or serve as a base type, though it can implement interfaces. | Supports class inheritance. | Can inherit only from another record. |
> | Typical fit | Small data-centric values with little behavior, such as a coordinate. | Entities with identity, a lifecycle or polymorphic behavior. | Data defined by its contents, such as messages or DTOs. |
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) · [Microsoft Learn: Classes (C# language specification)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes) · [Microsoft Learn: Records](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record)

# References

- [C# type system](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/)

---
topic: [Programming]
subtopic: [NET]
summary: "Type-safe, reusable code without duplicating logic per type, including constraints and variance."
level: ["4"]
priority: Medium
status: Ready to Repeat
publish: true
qard-deck: "Programming"
qard-topic: "NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Generics"
flashcard_uid: "3fc98b91"
created: "2026-02-18T20:04:43.000Z"
modified: "2026-11-02T09:03:54.806Z"
published: "2026-07-08T13:14:17.325Z"
---

Generics parameterize code by type. `List<T>` can store any `T` while the compiler still checks every read and write. That is a stronger contract than accepting `object` and recovering the real type with casts. For value types, generic collections also avoid the boxing required by older object-based APIs.

- `T` is a placeholder for a type chosen by the caller.
- `List<T>` is an open generic type definition. `List<int>` is a closed constructed type.
- Constraints (`where T : ...`) are capability contracts that unlock members safely.
- The runtime specializes generic code for value-type arguments and can share code between reference-type arguments.

# Use Cases

- Collections preserve the element or key type throughout an API.
- Algorithms can require only the operations they use, such as comparison or numeric operators.
- Generic result and handler types can keep payload types explicit without duplicating infrastructure.

A generic abstraction should still represent one real behavior. `IRepository<TEntity>` is not useful merely because every entity happens to support create, read, update, and delete operations. Different aggregates often need different contracts.

# Constraints

Constraints tell the compiler what operations are valid for `T`. They also document the smallest capability the algorithm expects.

- `where T : class` - `T` must be a reference type.
- `where T : struct` - `T` must be a non-nullable value type.
- `where T : notnull` - nullable analysis warns when a nullable type argument is used.
- `where T : unmanaged` - `T` is a non-nullable unmanaged type whose fields are also unmanaged. This is not identical to every platform's definition of blittable.
- `where T : new()` - `T` must have a public parameterless constructor.
- `where T : BaseType` - `T` must inherit from a specific base type.
- `where T : ISomeInterface` - `T` must implement a specific interface.

# Variance

Variance controls safe assignment between constructed interface or delegate types when their type arguments are related by inheritance.

- Invariance (default): `List<string>` is not assignable to `List<object>`.
- Covariance (`out T`): allows a more derived type where a base type is expected for producer-only APIs (for example, `IEnumerable<string>` to `IEnumerable<object>`).
- Contravariance (`in T`): allows a less derived type where a more derived type is expected for consumer-only APIs (for example, `IComparer<object>` as `IComparer<string>`).
- Variance is supported on interfaces and delegates marked with `in`/`out`, and only for reference-type substitutions.

```csharp
IEnumerable<string> names = new List<string> { "Ada", "Linus" };
IEnumerable<object> objects = names; // covariance

Action<object> printAny = o => Console.WriteLine(o);
Action<string> printString = printAny; // contravariance

List<string> list = new();
// List<object> invalid = list; // does not compile (invariance)
```

# Example

```csharp
public static T CreateAndValidate<T>()
    where T : EntityBase, IValidatable, new()
{
    var value = new T();
    value.Validate();
    return value;
}
```

# Generic Math (.NET 7+)

Generic code once had no static contract for operators such as `+`. Static abstract interface members changed that. `INumber<T>` declares numeric operators and identities, so a `where T : INumber<T>` constraint makes arithmetic available on the type parameter.

```csharp
public static T Sum<T>(ReadOnlySpan<T> values) where T : INumber<T>
{
    T total = T.Zero;
    foreach (var v in values) total += v;   // operators resolved via the interface
    return total;
}
```

The same static-member mechanism supports contracts such as `IParsable<TSelf>`, where parsing belongs to the type rather than an instance.

# Reflection over Generics

An open generic such as `List<>` has unassigned type parameters and cannot be instantiated. Reflection can close it at runtime with `MakeGenericType`. Generic methods use `MakeGenericMethod`.

```csharp
Type closed = typeof(List<>).MakeGenericType(itemType); // e.g. List<Order>
var list = Activator.CreateInstance(closed);
```

`where T : struct, Enum` admits enum value types, while `allows ref struct` tells the compiler that a type argument may be stack-only. Code using that anti-constraint must obey the ref-safety rules for every possible `T`.

# Pitfalls

- An unconstrained `T` exposes only operations valid for every type. The smallest constraint that the algorithm actually needs makes the required operations available without internal casts.
- **Static state belongs to each closed type.** `Cache<int>` and `Cache<string>` receive separate copies of a `static` field declared on `Cache<T>`.
- **Value-type specialization can grow native code.** Separate value-type instantiations can produce separate JIT-compiled bodies. The specialization avoids the boxing that `object`-based storage requires and preserves value semantics, but many large instantiations increase startup and code-size costs.
- `default(T)` is `null` for reference types and zero-initialized data for value types. Either result may look valid in a domain model, so absence should have an explicit contract.
- A concrete base-class constraint couples the abstraction to one hierarchy. A behavioral interface avoids that coupling when inheritance is not itself part of the requirement.

# Tradeoffs

- **Generics versus `object`.** Non-generic collections box value types when storing them as `object`. `List<int>` keeps integers unboxed and removes casts at the read boundary.
- **Generics versus inheritance.** A generic API carries a concrete type argument through compile-time checks. Inheritance allows one base reference to dispatch to different runtime implementations. The choice is about when variation is known, not a blanket performance rule.
- **Specialization versus code sharing.** The CLR normally specializes code for value-type arguments and shares compatible code for reference-type arguments. This balances value-type performance against native code size.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: 051626ec-488b-484a-affe-9b09e168fb5e -->
> [!qard]- What do generics add to a C# API?
> Generics let one implementation take a type as a parameter. The same code then works with many types, while the compiler still checks the type of every value that goes in or comes out.
>
> Compared with an API that accepts `object`:
>
> - **Type safety:** an `object`-based API needs casts on the way out, so a wrong type fails only at runtime. A `List<string>` instead rejects an `int` at compile time and returns strings without casts.
> - **No storage boxing for value types:** an `object`-based collection boxes each `int` it stores, while `List<int>` stores the integers directly. Generic code can still box a value-type `T` through conversions, such as converting it to `object` or to an interface type.
>
> **Constraints** such as `where T : IComparable<T>` narrow which type arguments are allowed. In return, the generic code may use the members that the constraint guarantees, such as `CompareTo`.
>
> [Microsoft: generic types and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft: constraints on type parameters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters) · [C# specification: boxing conversions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/conversions#1029-boxing-conversions)

<!-- qard-id: 96d2fdb0-3c95-4eb1-91da-258a4574cde2 -->
> [!qard]- Why does `IEnumerable<string>` assign to `IEnumerable<object>`, but `List<string>` does not assign to `List<object>`?
> `IEnumerable<T>` declares its type parameter covariant (`out T`), so the conversion is allowed. `List<T>` is invariant, so it is not.
>
> - **`IEnumerable<string>` as `IEnumerable<object>`:** the interface only hands `T` values out. Every string read from the sequence is also an object, so reading strings as objects is safe.
> - **`List<string>` as `List<object>`:** `List<T>` also takes `T` values in, for example through `Add`. If the conversion were allowed, code could add an `int` through the `List<object>` reference, and the original `List<string>` would then hold a non-string.
>
> Variance also has to be declared, and C# allows it only on generic interfaces and delegates. A generic class such as `List<T>` is therefore always invariant, whatever its members do.
>
> [Microsoft: covariance and contravariance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/covariance-and-contravariance)

<!-- qard-id: 222e6ef2-bb7d-4c83-b731-ffd892537b23 -->
> [!qard]- When should a generic interface type parameter be marked `out` or `in`?
> A type parameter can be marked `out` when the interface only produces `T`, and `in` when it only consumes `T`. When `T` flows both in and out, it stays invariant.
>
> | Marking | Where `T` may appear | Conversion it enables |
> |---|---|---|
> | `out` (covariant) | Only in output positions, such as method return types | A more derived type argument can stand in for a less derived one: `IEnumerable<string>` converts to `IEnumerable<object>` |
> | `in` (contravariant) | Only in input positions, such as method parameter types | A less derived type argument can stand in for a more derived one: `IComparer<object>` converts to `IComparer<string>` |
> | None (invariant) | In both input and output positions | No conversion, because either direction would allow an unsafe read or write |
>
> The compiler enforces these positions, so it accepts a variant marking only when the interface's members keep it safe.
>
> Variance conversions work only when the type arguments are reference types. `IEnumerable<int>` does not convert to `IEnumerable<object>`, because a value-type argument makes the constructed type invariant.
>
> [Microsoft: covariance and contravariance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/covariance-and-contravariance)

<!-- qard-id: dd86df45-1404-46cf-8c09-84cb046ef4f3 -->
> [!qard]- A generic method uses `default(T)` as a fallback. Why can this be dangerous?
> `default(T)` is not one fixed value. It is `null` when `T` is a reference type, and a zero-initialized value such as `0` or `false` when `T` is a value type. Those values can also be legitimate data, so returning `default(T)` to signal that nothing was found or that something failed makes absence look like a real result.
>
> For example, a `GetOrDefault<T>` method that returns `default(T)` for a missing key returns `0` when `T` is `int`. A caller then cannot tell a missing entry from a stored `0`.
>
> When that distinction matters, the API reports absence separately from the value:
>
> - **`Try` method:** returns `bool` for success and the value through an `out T` parameter.
> - **Result type:** carries the success or failure state together with the value.
> - **Nullable contract:** returns `T?`, with `null` meaning absence. This works only when `null` is never legitimate data and the return type can actually hold `null` for the type argument. For a value type that requires `Nullable<T>`, for example `T?` under a `where T : struct` constraint, whose `HasValue` separates a missing entry from a stored `0`. With an unconstrained `T`, `T?` adds no null state for a value-type argument, so `GetOrDefault<int>` would still return `0`.
>
> [Microsoft: default keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/default) · [Microsoft: nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types)

> [!qard]- Do different closed forms of a generic type share its static fields?
> No. `Cache<int>` and `Cache<string>` have separate copies of every static field declared on `Cache<T>`. Incrementing `Cache<int>.Count` leaves `Cache<string>.Count` unchanged. This separation follows type identity and does not depend on whether the CLR shares native method code between compatible instantiations. A per-type cache can use it deliberately; a process-wide total must live outside that generic type's per-instantiation state. [Microsoft: generic classes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/generic-classes)

# References

- [Generics in C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/)
- [Covariance and contravariance in C#](https://ericlippert.com/2007/10/16/covariance-and-contravariance-in-c-part-1/)

---
topic: [AI & ML]
subtopic: [LLM]
summary: "Deliberately deciding what fills the finite context window, and in what order, to maximize useful signal."
tags: [FolderNote]
level: ["2"]
priority: High
status: Done
publish: true
qard-deck: "AI & ML"
qard-topic: "LLM/Context Engineering/Context Engineering"
flashcard_uid: "0d1d06bc"
created: "2026-06-11T07:39:53.000Z"
modified: "2026-10-28T12:33:42.000Z"
published: "2026-07-13T18:58:50.735Z"
---

Context engineering decides what the model sees and where it appears in the context window. Instructions compete with examples, retrieved evidence, conversation history, and tool traffic for the same finite budget. Once a system gains retrieval or memory, [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Prompt Engineering|Prompting]] is only one part of an assembled payload.

On the [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/LLM|engineering ladder]], context engineering sits between the instruction and the runtime around it. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Harness Engineering|Harness Engineering]] controls what the model can do. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Loop Engineering|Loop Engineering]] controls repeated behavior. Context engineering controls the material available for each decision.

The hard constraint is uneven attention inside a limited window. Models tend to use evidence near the beginning and end better than evidence buried in the middle. And answer quality can decline as otherwise relevant input grows, often called context rot. More context is therefore a poor default. The target is the smallest well-ordered context that still contains the evidence needed for the task.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph CW[Context window -- finite shared budget]
      SP[System prompt]
      H[Conversation history]
      RC[Retrieved evidence]
      TS[Tool schemas and results]
      O[Reserved output space]
    end
    SP --> M[Model attention]
    H --> M
    RC --> M
    TS --> M
```

Retrieval is the main way external evidence enters the window. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Context Engineering/RAG/RAG|RAG]] selects and ranks that evidence, then bounds how much of it reaches generation.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# The Context Budget

The system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool schemas, tool results, and reserved output space all draw from one token budget. They are accounted for like memory allocations. Deciding what to remove before the total reaches the limit keeps the runtime from truncating an old instruction by accident.

Three costs are easy to miss:

- Output needs headroom. The `max_tokens` budget comes from what remains after the input. [[Generation]] cannot produce tokens that the context limit has already consumed.
- Tool schemas are sent as input. Names, descriptions, and parameter definitions can consume thousands of tokens before the first call. [[Tool Design]] covers the accuracy cost of oversized toolsets.
- History grows every turn. Reasoning, calls, and results quietly fill the window during long [[Agent Loop|agent loops]] unless the runtime compacts them.

# Techniques

**Ordering and positioning.** The strongest instructions and evidence go where the model is most likely to use them, usually near the start or end. Ranked retrieval should place its best chunk first. This is the context-assembly side of [[Generation]].

**Selection over stuffing.** A few complete, relevant chunks usually beat a pile of fragments. [[Retrieval]] keeps the candidate set focused, while [[Re-ranking|Reranking]] spends extra work to choose what actually enters the prompt.

**Compaction.** Old turns are replaced with a short record of decisions, constraints, and pending work before history crowds out the task. Tool results should return only fields used by the next decision. [[Tool Design]] shows how oversized API payloads consume context without improving the next decision. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Loop Engineering/Loop Engineering|Loop Engineering]] turns token pressure into an explicit compact-or-stop condition.

**Rebuild instead of replay.** A long-lived agent can keep the raw transcript outside the context window. Each turn is rebuilt from the policies, stable preferences, recalled facts or episodes, and recent activity that matter now. The transcript remains evidence, but it does not automatically return to the prompt. The [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Agents/Agents#Memory Systems|memory system]] decides what may persist. Context engineering decides what belongs in this call.

**Structure.** Explicit sections separate trusted instructions from untrusted data. That makes the payload easier to interpret and supports [[Guardrails|prompt injection]] defenses. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Prompt Engineering|prompt anatomy]] supplies the smaller building blocks.

**Offloading.** Bulky intermediate state is stored outside the window, and the context carries a lightweight reference to it. A scratchpad or file can hold detail that is needed later but not on every turn. [[Multi-Agentic Systems]] uses the same idea for shared artifacts.

**Isolation.** Work is split into separate contexts when two concerns need conflicting instructions or large, unrelated toolsets. The context-centric decomposition in [[Multi-Agentic Systems]] keeps each worker's window focused, though coordination adds cost.

**Caching stable prefixes.** A repeated system prompt or fixed tool definition can stay logically present without paying full processing cost each time. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/LLM Caching#Prompt Caching|Prompt Caching]] covers prefix layout, provider boundaries, and verification of actual reuse.

# Pitfalls

## More Context, Worse Answers

**What goes wrong:** more retrieved documents or a longer system prompt lowers answer quality and raises latency.

**Why it happens:** useful evidence is diluted across the larger input, and some of it lands in the weakly attended middle. Irrelevant tokens still compete for attention.

**How to avoid it:** filtering and reranking reduce the evidence to a smaller set, and quality is measured as context size changes. Added tokens are worth keeping only while they still improve the result.

## Unbounded History Growth

**What goes wrong:** a long run fills the window, after which the runtime drops old messages or rejects the request. The original instruction is often among the first things lost.

**Why it happens:** each iteration appends reasoning and raw tool output without compaction.

**How to avoid it:** tool-result size is capped and cumulative tokens are tracked per iteration, so the runtime compacts or stops before the limit. [[Agent Loop]] traces how repeated oversized results become token explosion across iterations.

## Context Poisoning

**What goes wrong:** one hallucinated fact or injected instruction enters history and is replayed as trusted context on later turns.

**Why it happens:** the runtime replays history without a trust label, and natural-language errors carry no automatic warning.

**How to avoid it:** claims are validated before storage, untrusted content stays separate from instructions, and controls are enforced in code. [[Guardrails]] should not depend on a poisoned prompt obeying itself.

## Tool-Schema Bloat

**What goes wrong:** attaching many tools inflates every request and makes selection less reliable.

**Why it happens:** many clients send every connected schema on every request, even when the task needs only one.

**How to avoid it:** each request exposes only the tools the current task needs, or tool search loads them on demand. [[Tool Design]] covers the degradation seen with large toolsets.

# Tradeoffs

| Lever | What it buys | What it costs | Best when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Larger context window | More room before truncation | Longer actual input, not the larger limit itself, raises token cost and, depending on model, task and implementation, can lower answer quality and add latency | The task truly needs broad material at once |
| Retrieval + reranking | Dense and traceable evidence | Retrieval infrastructure and tuning | Knowledge-heavy tasks over a large corpus |
| History compaction | A bounded window over long sessions | Summary cost and possible detail loss | Long conversations and agent runs |
| Context offloading | Small working context with detail on demand | Extra reads and coordination | Multi-step work with bulky intermediate state |
| Context isolation (sub-agents) | A focused window for each concern | Coordination overhead and more total tokens | Conflicting instructions or oversized toolsets |

The smallest context that answers the task is the starting point. Retrieval and reranking control what enters, and compaction frees space before more capacity is added. Offloading or isolation becomes worthwhile only when one focused window cannot hold the work. Once extra context stops improving measured quality, it has become overhead.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: ddd8a30b-97ea-4f04-8025-704d1c3481ab -->
> [!qard]- Why can adding more context make answers worse instead of better?
> Because a model does not use every part of a long input equally well, so extra material can bury or dilute the evidence that the answer depends on.
>
> - **Position effects:** in the long-context tasks evaluated in *Lost in the Middle*, some models used relevant information near the beginning or end of the input more reliably than the same information placed in the middle. The size of the effect depends on the model and task.
> - **Dilution:** irrelevant or redundant text competes with the useful evidence, so adding it can lower answer quality instead of adding information.
> - **Cost:** extra input tokens also add cost and can add latency, even when they do not improve the answer.
>
> Added context is not always harmful. The aim is complete, relevant material placed deliberately, with answer quality and input cost measured on the actual workload as the context grows.
>
> [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172) · [Latency optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization)

<!-- qard-id: ed47de12-495f-495b-8cbb-662c952b3224 -->
> [!qard]- How can a long-running agent keep useful context within a finite window?
> By treating the context window as a working set. Each call contains the instructions, evidence and state needed for the next decision. Everything else stays outside the prompt but remains retrievable.
>
> The prompt, conversation history, tool results and space reserved for the response all draw from one finite token budget, so they are managed together:
>
> - **Selection and ordering:** only material relevant to the current step enters the window, and it is placed deliberately rather than replayed in full.
> - **Trimmed tool results:** tool output keeps the fields the next decision uses, and stale results that no longer matter are cleared.
> - **Compaction:** older turns are replaced by a short record of decisions, constraints and open work before history crowds out the task.
> - **Offloading:** bulky state, such as notes, files or full documents, lives outside the prompt and is reloaded by reference when needed.
>
> Compaction trades space for possible detail loss: a summary can drop a subtle fact that later matters. Where exact recovery matters, the source material is kept outside the window instead of being trusted to the summary.
>
> [Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)

# References

- [Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (Liu et al., 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)
- [Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic Engineering)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
- [Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance (Chroma Research)](https://research.trychroma.com/context-rot)

Loop engineering designs the runtime around repeated model calls. It controls the observe → decide → act cycle, defines when work is finished, checks progress between steps, and hands uncertain decisions to a person.

A single call is bounded. A loop carries each result into the next iteration, so mistakes can accumulate just as easily as useful progress. Good loop design keeps small errors small. Model quality alone cannot do that.

This is the last rung of the runtime stack. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Prompt Engineering/Prompt Engineering|Prompt Engineering]] shapes one instruction. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Context Engineering/Context Engineering|Context Engineering]] shapes what the model sees, while [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Harness Engineering/Harness Engineering|Harness Engineering]] controls what it can do. Loop engineering adds time: how behavior develops across turns. [[Agent Loop]] covers the mechanics of that cycle, and [[Multi-Agentic Systems]] covers coordination among several loops.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Termination and Budgets

An agent loop has no natural end. It can keep calling tools for as long as the runtime asks for another step, with every weak result becoming input to the next one. Hard bounds belong in the initial design.

- **Iteration caps** set a hard per-request limit on loop cycles. The cap is the final defense against an infinite tool-call sequence. [[Agent Loop]] shows concrete framework controls and the failure they prevent.
- **Token and cost budgets** track cumulative use and stop or compact the run before it exhausts the context window or spend ceiling.
- **Checkable stop criteria** separate stopping from success. A turn with no remaining tool calls shows only that the model has stopped requesting actions; completion needs task-specific evidence the runtime can verify, such as a passing test suite or a schema-valid artifact. Instructions to stop may help, but they do not replace hard limits.
- **A budget fallback** determines what happens at the cap. The runtime can return the best partial result with a warning or escalate to a person. Silent truncation hides the failure.

# Verification Inside the Loop

A loop that only generates will drift. Verification turns each iteration into a chance to recover.

- **Gates between steps** validate an intermediate result before another iteration consumes it. A rejected schema or failed output check should return a clear error that the next pass can act on.
- **Self-checks** use a second model pass to compare a draft with explicit criteria and feed revisions back. This is the evaluator-optimizer pattern described in [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Agents/Agents|Agents]].
- **Ground-truth signals** give the strongest feedback: a test passes, code compiles, or a claim traces to a source. Loops work best when success is externally checkable. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Agents/Evaluation/Evaluation|Agent Evaluation]] covers trajectory quality and reliability across stochastic runs.
- **Human escape hatches** pause work when an action is irreversible or its result cannot be checked safely. [[Guardrails]] explains why the boundary must live in code and infrastructure rather than the prompt.

# State Across Iterations

Each iteration adds calls and results to the history. Without intervention, context grows until the runtime truncates it or the model reaches its limit. [[Home/AI & ML/LLM/Context Engineering/Context Engineering|Context Engineering]] decides what belongs in the window. Loop engineering decides when to compact, offload, or stop.

- **Compaction cadence** schedules summaries against a token threshold before overflow removes old, potentially important messages.
- **Offloading between turns** moves large artifacts to external storage and keeps lightweight references in context. [[Multi-Agentic Systems]] uses the same filesystem-artifact pattern for handoffs.
- **State outside the window** gives the loop a durable plan or progress log to reread after compaction. Long runs remain tied to the original goal even when early turns have been summarized away.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: 638a8ef2-9d81-4a06-a5d4-43fd0f3c5d3e -->
> [!qard]- What does a tool-using model need from a runtime to operate as a loop?
> The runtime executes requested tools, returns observations to the model, and decides whether another turn runs. It owns the completion check and operational bounds; the model’s final text alone does not prove the task succeeded. A one-call tool request becomes a loop only when the runtime sends its result back for another decision. [Claude tool-use loop](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works)

<!-- qard-id: 599da810-5eee-4ed5-ae4b-95b2737c4d8f -->
> [!qard]- What should a runtime report when its loop budget expires before the task is complete?
> The runtime reports that the run stopped incomplete, not that it succeeded. The report names the limit that was reached, the completion condition that is still unmet, and the partial result or state produced so far.
>
> - **Why it matters:** budget exhaustion is not success. If partial output is presented as a final answer or silently truncated, callers treat unfinished work as done and the failure stays hidden.
> - **What follows:** where the application configures it, the partial state and the unresolved work pass to a continuation run or to a person. Otherwise the run ends with an explicit error.
>
> Platform behavior differs. The OpenAI Agents SDK treats reaching `max_turns` as an error condition and supports a handler for that case. With Anthropic task budgets, a task that exceeds its budget can end with a partial result.
>
> Sources: [OpenAI Agents SDK: Running agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/) · [Anthropic task budgets](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/task-budgets)

<!-- qard-id: 29510b5e-892b-49d6-9b58-c95c4a2ba3d4 -->
> [!qard]- In a long-running agent, how is compaction work split between deciding what context to keep and deciding when to compact?
> Compaction needs two separate decisions. The content decision, owned by context engineering, determines what the model still needs and what a summary must preserve. The timing decision, owned by loop engineering, determines when to compact, offload an artifact or stop. Compaction typically runs at a token threshold, before the next request would overflow the window.
>
> | Decision | What it settles | Failure when it is neglected |
> |---|---|---|
> | Content (context engineering) | Which goals, decisions, open issues and references a summary keeps | The summary drops a constraint, and later turns proceed without it |
> | Timing (loop engineering) | When to summarize, when to move large artifacts to external storage behind lightweight references, and when to stop | The window overflows, and truncation removes old messages that may still matter |
>
> Durable state sits outside both decisions. A plan or progress log stored by the application can be reread after compaction, which keeps a long run tied to its original goal. OpenAI Responses API compaction, for example, carries prior state forward as smaller, opaque compaction items. Plans and artifacts that the application must rely on remain application-managed.
>
> This split is a convention for assigning responsibility, not a boundary defined by an API.
>
> Source: [OpenAI: Compaction](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/compaction)
